hints: Start from the ion before water is involved and think about its state, then think about the state after it is surrounded by water.
walkthrough:
Picture what hydration means**
Imagine a single isolated ion floating in the gas phase, like $\text{K}^{+}(\text{g})$. Now drop it into a beaker of water. Water molecules crowd around it and form ion-dipole bonds to it. Hydration is exactly that change from $\text{g}$ to $\text{aq}$.

Build the precise definition**
A standard enthalpy always refers to one mole. So you say: the energy change when one mole of gaseous ions dissolves in water to give aqueous ions, for example $\text{K}^{+}(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{K}^{+}(\text{aq})$. Bond forming to water releases energy, so $\Delta H_{hyd}$ is exothermic.
Final answer: The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous ions dissolves in water to form aqueous ions.

hints: Compare the charges and sizes of $\text{K}^{+}$ and $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and recall how charge density controls attraction strength.
Link stronger attraction for the partial negative oxygen in $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ to more energy released on hydration.
walkthrough:
Compare the ions side by side**
$\text{K}^{+}$ is $1+$ and relatively large. $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ is $2+$ and smaller. That means $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ packs twice the charge into a smaller volume. In other words, $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ has a much higher charge density than $\text{K}^{+}$.

Link charge density to water attraction**
Hydration energy comes from forming ion-dipole bonds between the ion and water molecules, mainly to the $\delta-$ oxygen atom of $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. A higher charge density ion pulls those water molecules much more strongly. So $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ attracts $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ more strongly than $\text{K}^{+}$ does.

Explain the numbers**
Stronger bonds to water mean more energy is released. That is why $\Delta H_{hyd}$ for $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ is $-1650 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ compared with only $-322 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ for $\text{K}^{+}$.

Final answer: $\text{K}^{+}$ has a larger ionic radius and a smaller charge than $\text{Ca}^{2+}$, so $\text{K}^{+}$ has a lower charge density.
$\text{Ca}^{2+}$ therefore exerts a stronger attraction for $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ molecules and releases more energy on hydration, so $\Delta H_{hyd}$ of $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ is more exothermic.

hints: Think of the reverse of breaking a lattice apart, starting from separated gaseous ions and ending with the ordered solid.
walkthrough:
Picture lattice formation**
Imagine $\text{Ca}^{2+}(\text{g})$ and $\text{F}^{-}(\text{g})$ far apart. Now let them come together into the regular 3D arrangement of solid $\text{CaF}_{2}(\text{s})$. Huge electrostatic attraction is set up and a lot of energy is released.

State the molar definition**
Lattice energy $\Delta H_{latt}$ is the energy change when one mole of ionic solid forms from its gaseous ions, for example $\text{Ca}^{2+}(\text{g}) + 2\text{F}^{-}(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{CaF}_{2}(\text{s})$.
Final answer: The energy change when one mole of solid ionic compound is formed from its gaseous ions.

hints: Draw the Hess route: $\text{CaF}_{2}(\text{s})$ to gaseous ions is the reverse of lattice formation, then hydrate one $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and two $\text{F}^{-}$ ions.
Remember to multiply the $\text{F}^{-}$ hydration value by 2 because the formula is $\text{CaF}_{2}$, then combine with $-\Delta H_{latt}$.
walkthrough:
Set up the Hess cycle in your head**
Dissolving is a two stage route: first break the lattice into gaseous ions, then hydrate those ions. Breaking the lattice is the opposite of lattice formation, so its enthalpy is $-\Delta H_{latt} = -(-2602) = +2602 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Add the hydration steps with correct moles**
One mole of $\text{CaF}_{2}$ gives one $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and two $\text{F}^{-}$ ions. So total hydration enthalpy is: $$\Delta H_{hyd, total} = -1650 + 2 \times (-506) = -1650 -1012 = -2662 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Combine to get solution enthalpy**
Add the two stages: $$\Delta H_{sol} = +2602 + (-2662) = -60 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ The slightly exothermic result makes sense because the very exothermic hydration just outweighs the energy needed to break the lattice.

Final answer: $$\Delta H_{sol} = -\Delta H_{latt} + \Delta H_{hyd}(\text{Ca}^{2+}) + 2\Delta H_{hyd}(\text{F}^{-})$$
$$= +2602 -1650 + 2(-506) = -60 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

hints: Start from $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ and rearrange to make $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ the subject with $T = 298 \text{ K}$.
Watch the units: $\Delta H^{\ominus}$ and $\Delta G^{\ominus}$ are in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ but $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ is required in $\text{J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$, so convert by $\times 1000$.
walkthrough:
Rearrange the Gibbs equation**
You know $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$. Rearranging for entropy gives: $$\Delta S^{\ominus} = \frac{\Delta H^{\ominus} - \Delta G^{\ominus}}{T}$$ Temperature must be in kelvin, so $T = 298 \text{ K}$.

Substitute and handle units carefully**
$$\Delta H^{\ominus} - \Delta G^{\ominus} = -1214 - (-1162) = -52 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ Convert to joules: $-52 \times 1000 = -52000 \text{ J mol}^{-1}$. Then: $$\Delta S^{\ominus} = \frac{-52000}{298} = -174.5 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$$

Sense check the sign**
The reaction is $\text{Ca(s)} + \text{F}_{2}(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{CaF}_{2}(\text{s})$. A gas is consumed to make a solid, so disorder decreases. A negative $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ is exactly what you expect.

Final answer: $$\Delta S^{\ominus} = \frac{\Delta H^{\ominus} - \Delta G^{\ominus}}{T} = \frac{-1214 - (-1162)}{298} \times 1000$$
$$= -174.5 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$$
